On Form T661, repayments are added back to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool on Line 445 and to qualified expenditures for investment tax credit purposes on Line 560.

Canada's research and development (R&D) tax incentive ecosystem—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program and complemented by ten provincial and territorial tax credit regimes—has undergone its most comprehensive statutory transformation in over a decade.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, federal and provincial lawmakers enacted sweeping structural reforms that render pre-2025 compliance manuals obsolete. Federally, following the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), the August 15, 2025 draft legislative proposals, and the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget tabled by Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, these amendments doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual cash refund from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million, which Canadian-controlled private corporations [CCPCs] may also elect to use), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Operationally, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process providing upfront eligibility determinations within eight weeks and cutting post-filing expenditure review service standards from 180 days to 90 days. Furthermore, CPA firm analyses of the November 5, 2026 Federal Budget indicate a proposed expansion of SR&ED eligibility to include post-laboratory commercialization costs—specifically initial regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) protection expenses—effective late 2026.

At the provincial level, two jurisdictions executed landmark structural shifts while others retained independent parameters. In Québec, the March 25, 2025 provincial budget abolished legacy R&D tax credits and holidays, consolidating provincial innovation support into the new, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, which provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures (including capital property) above an exclusion threshold, and 20% on excess expenditures. In British Columbia, the provincial government expressly aligned with the federal Bill C-15 reforms—raising its 10% refundable SR&ED expenditure limit to $6,000,000, admitting ECPCs, and restoring capital expenditures—while BC Budget 2026 permanently eliminated the credit's statutory sunset clause. Conversely, Ontario (retaining its $3,000,000 cap on the 8% refundable OITC and 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC) and Alberta (retaining its $4,000,000 cap on the 8%/20% Innovation Employment Grant) maintained independent calculation bases.
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture

Canada's federal SR&ED program is not a discretionary grant scheme; it is a statutory entitlement embedded within the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (ITA) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (ITR). The statutory architecture operates as a dual-mechanism incentive. First, under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers may pool allowable current and (post-December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada under subsection 37(1) to deduct against current-year income for tax purposes or carry forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Second, under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers earn a federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) on their "qualified expenditures" at a basic rate of 15% or an enhanced rate of 35%, which reduces Part I federal tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5), can be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years, or—for qualifying claimants under section 127.1—is paid out as a direct cash refund.
1.1 Core Statutory Provisions of the Income Tax Act and Regulations

A rigorous audit of any Canadian R&D tax claim requires cross-referencing the specific subsections of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations that govern technical eligibility, expenditure pooling, credit computation, refundability, and anti-avoidance.

body.text: 2. Technical Eligibility Framework: The "Why" and "How" Requirements

To qualify for federal and provincial R&D incentives, work must satisfy the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. While the statutory wording of subsection 248(1) has remained stable since the 1990s, the CRA's administrative framework for evaluating technical eligibility has evolved through three distinct eras. First, from 1986 to 2012, following the May 1985 federal budget's introduction of "experimental development" to replace Interpretation Bulletin IT-439, Revenue Canada issued Information Circular IC 86-4 and its 1994 revision IC 86-4R3 (now archived), which established the three foundational pillars of industrial SR&ED: scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and scientific and technical content. Second, from 2012 to 2021, the CRA published the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (issued December 19, 2012, revised April 24, 2015, and archived August 13, 2021), which codified the judicial test from Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839) into a formal Two-Step methodology centred on five sequential questions. Third, on August 13, 2021, following its 2020 modernization review, the CRA replaced the archived 2012/2015 policy with the current Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. The 2021 Guidelines streamline the five jurisprudential questions into two core statutory requirements derived directly from subsection 248(1): the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement. As confirmed by both the CRA and the Tax Court of Canada in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025), the 2021 Guidelines did not alter the law; the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the governing legal standard embedded within the "Why" and "How" framework.
2.1 The "Why" Requirement: Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty

The "Why" Requirement examines the objective purpose of the work: it must be undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge (basic or applied research) or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement (experimental development). Eligible SR&ED seeks to generate or discover conceptual knowledge—such as new scientific theories, predictive models, or understanding of underlying technological relationships—rather than merely collecting factual measurements or applying established engineering techniques. Crucially, a scientific or technological advancement cannot be sought unless the project encounters a scientific or technological uncertainty. Uncertainty exists when it is unknown or unpredictable whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, due to an insufficiency in the combined available scientific or technological knowledge. This baseline of available knowledge comprises both the internal knowledge and experience of the claimant's qualified personnel and all publicly accessible knowledge in the relevant field of science or technology.
In experimental development—the most frequently claimed category—the CRA's 2021 Guidelines recognize seven primary indicators that the existing technological knowledge base is insufficient:

items: Existing design methods or engineering procedures are inapplicable to the problem.
Performance requirements or specifications deviate beyond existing industry standards.
The system involves too many interacting variables or unknowns to predict behaviour mathematically or empirically.
Operating parameters or environmental conditions fall outside normal operating ranges.
The nature of the technical problem evolves dynamically during the investigation.
Necessary empirical data is not readily available and cannot be obtained by routine measurement.
The project faces interlocking constraints where improving one parameter degrades another in an unpredictable manner.

body.text: If a technical team encounters an obstacle and circumvents it using a standard workaround drawn from available knowledge, or merely acquires existing know-how through employee training, hiring external specialists, or purchasing off-the-shelf proprietary software, no technological advancement occurs. Similarly, attempting to meet a commercial cost target does not, by itself, create technological uncertainty unless achieving that cost target within project constraints forces the claimant to overcome underlying physical, material, or architectural limitations. Because the SR&ED program rewards the generation of scientific or technological knowledge rather than commercial viability, success or failure in achieving the project's technical or commercial objective is irrelevant to meeting the "Why" requirement. Proving through rigorous experimentation that a hypothesized technological approach cannot work under specific constraints constitutes a valid technological advancement.
2.2 The "How" Requirement: Systematic Investigation or Search

The "How" Requirement governs the methodology used to resolve the uncertainty: the work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Merely working in an organized, professional, or iterative manner—such as executing standard Agile software development sprints or conducting unguided trial-and-error troubleshooting—does not satisfy the "How" requirement. Instead, the investigation must adhere to the scientific method across four mandatory steps:

items: Formulation of a Hypothesis: Generating a specific idea, proposed solution, or causal model consistent with known scientific or technological facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation.

Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the idea or hypothesis through structured experiments or mathematical/engineering analysis, where the hypothesis can evolve and change as a result of testing.
Development of Logical Conclusions: Evaluating the experimental or analytical findings against the hypothesis to formulate logical conclusions about why the system behaved as it did.
Keeping of Contemporaneous Evidence: Generating and retaining documentary evidence of the hypotheses tested and the results obtained as the work progresses.

body.text: 2.3 Mapping the Five Northwest Hydraulic Questions to the 2021 Guidelines

During CRA technical reviews—conducted by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) pursuant to the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors—and Tax Court litigation, the CRA's "Why" and "How" requirements map directly onto the five questions established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen:

headers: Core Evidentiary Burden on the Claimant

cells: Question 1: Was there a scientific or a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?

Demonstrate an insufficiency in combined internal and publicly available knowledge (e.g., system-level architectural bottlenecks, interlocking constraints) rather than a mere lack of internal familiarity.
Question 2: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Identify specific, testable scientific or technological hypotheses formulated prior to testing, rather than random trial-and-error or brute-force parameter tuning.
Question 3: Did the overall procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including formulating, testing, and modifying the hypotheses by experiment or analysis?
Prove that variables were controlled, metrics were measured systematically, and results were analyzed to form logical conclusions driving subsequent iterations.
Question 4: Did the process result in a scientific or a technological advancement (or was it undertaken for that purpose)?
Articulate the new conceptual scientific or technological knowledge gained regarding underlying principles, relationships, or capabilities (even if the prototype failed commercially).
Question 5: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?
Produce dated, contemporaneous artifacts (e.g., architecture diagrams, load testing metrics, latency logs, iteration histories, lab notebooks, time records) created during the taxation year.

body.text: 2.4 Categories of Eligible Work, Support Work, and Statutory Exclusions

Subsection 248(1) divides eligible work into three primary research categories (paragraphs (a), (b), and (c)) and one derivative category (paragraph (d)), while strictly excluding seven categories of commercial or routine activity (paragraphs (e) through (k)). Basic research (paragraph 248(1)(a)) comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, such as investigating fundamental properties of elementary particles or a newly discovered virus. Applied research (paragraph 248(1)(b)) comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, such as developing a vaccine against a newly discovered virus. Experimental development (paragraph 248(1)(c)) comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements.

Derivative support work (paragraph 248(1)(d)) is not SR&ED on its own. It qualifies only if it meets two cumulative statutory conditions: first, it must fall within one of eight exhaustive statutory disciplines—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—and second, it must be commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada. Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k) explicitly exclude seven categories of ineligible work:

items: Market research or sales promotion (paragraph (e)).
Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes (paragraph (f)).
Research in the social sciences or the humanities (paragraph (g)).
Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas (paragraph (h)).
The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process (paragraph (i)).
Style changes (paragraph (j)).
Routine data collection (paragraph (k)).

body.text: As the CRA's 2021 Guidelines emphasize, distinguishing eligible support work (such as "data collection" or "testing" under paragraph (d)) from excluded work (such as "routine data collection" under paragraph (k) or "routine testing" under paragraph (f)) depends entirely on purpose. Routine data collection or testing carried out for standard operational quality control is excluded under paragraphs (f) and (k), whereas data collection or testing carried out specifically to validate a hypothesis within an active experimental development investigation is eligible as support work under paragraph (d).
2.5 Prototypes, Pilot Plants, and Shop-Floor Production Runs

When experimental development moves out of the laboratory and onto the manufacturing shop floor or involves physical asset construction, two specialized CRA policies govern the boundary between eligible SR&ED and excluded commercial production. Under the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy, designing, constructing, and testing a prototype or operating a non-commercial pilot plant to verify a hypothesis or resolve technological uncertainty constitutes eligible experimental development. Because a pure prototype usually has no commercial application or limited value once tested, the labour and materials used in its development are treated as current SR&ED expenditures and materials consumed. However, if the input materials forming part of the prototype or pilot plant retain value and are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, they are treated as materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED and become subject to ITC recapture under subsection 127(27). Work and expenditures normally associated with building a commercial plant had the technology already existed do not qualify.

Similarly, under the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, when experimental trials occur on a commercial production line, the CRA evaluates technical factors and contemporaneous records to determine whether the context of each production run is Experimental Development with Experimental Production (ED+EP) or Experimental Development with Commercial Production (ED+CP). If the technical considerations and available evidence do not establish that the production run is ED+EP, the context defaults to ED+CP. Any production beyond what is strictly required for the SR&ED is classified as excess production; all labour, overhead, and material costs attributable to commercial production or excess production are disallowed.
3. Federal ITC Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Out Formulas, and Refundability

The federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit regime under sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act operates on a two-tier rate structure: a 15% basic rate available to all eligible taxpayers and an enhanced 35% rate (comprising the 15% basic ITC plus an additional 20% ITC under subsection 127(10.1)) available to qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) and—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) up to their annual expenditure limit.
3.1 The 2024–2026 Legislative Evolution: From $3M to $4.5M to $6M

A critical audit verification point involves tracking the three-stage legislative progression between late 2024 and March 2026. Under the historical pre-reform regime (for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024), only CCPCs qualified for the 35% enhanced rate, capped at an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (yielding up to $1,050,000 in refundable ITCs), which phased out on a straight-line basis when the associated group's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada lay between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, while capital expenditures acquired after December 31, 2013, and before December 16, 2024, were excluded.

In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and the August 15, 2025 draft legislative proposals released by the Department of Finance, the federal government initially proposed increasing the enhanced expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000 (raising maximum annual refundable ITCs to $1,575,000), expanding the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extending the 35% refundable rate to ECPCs (phased out over $15M–$75M of three-year average gross revenue), allowing CCPCs to elect into the gross revenue phase-out formula, and restoring capital expenditures and lease costs after December 15, 2024. Subsequently, on November 4, 2025, Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne presented Federal Budget 2025, which confirmed all structural reforms from the August 2025 draft legislation and further increased the annual enhanced expenditure limit from the proposed $4,500,000 to $6,000,000, retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Enacted into law via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit allows qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs to earn up to $2,100,000 per year in refundable enhanced federal ITCs.
3.2 Statutory Definition of Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)

Under the amended definitions in subsections 127(9) and 89(1) of the Income Tax Act, a corporation qualifies as an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) for a taxation year beginning on or after December 16, 2024, if, throughout the taxation year, it satisfies three cumulative statutory conditions:

items: It is resident in Canada.

It is a public corporation as defined in subsection 89(1) (meaning its shares are listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada or internationally, or it has elected or been designated to be a public corporation).

It is not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons. Consequently, a Canadian subsidiary of a foreign multinational or a Canadian public company controlled by non-resident shareholders is excluded from ECPC status and remains restricted to the 15% non-refundable basic rate.

body.text: 3.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas (Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue)

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit—which must be shared among associated CCPCs using Schedule T2SCH49 or among consolidated ECPC corporate groups under subsections 127(10.61) to (10.64)—phases out on a straight-line basis between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 under two statutory methodologies.
Method 1: Taxable Capital Employed in Canada (Default for CCPCs — ITA s. 127(10.2))

Unless a CCPC elects otherwise, its $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced based on the taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation (and all associated corporations) for the immediately preceding taxation year. Once prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000, the expenditure limit decreases on a straight-line basis and becomes nil ($0) once taxable capital reaches $75,000,000:

where A is nil ($0) if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is ≤ $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000. (For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the maximum limit was $3,000,000 and phased out over a $40,000,000 range between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital).
Method 2: Three-Year Average Gross Revenue (Mandatory for ECPCs & Elective for CCPCs — ITA s. 127(10.6))

Under subsection 127(10.6), an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis when the corporation's average annual gross revenue (determined on a consolidated basis at the highest level of consolidation presented to shareholders, or standard GAAP financial statements for single entities) over the three preceding fiscal years (or the actual one or two preceding fiscal years if fewer than three exist under subsection 127(10.62)) lies between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Crucially, a CCPC (or associated group of CCPCs) may file an election on the prescribed form to have its expenditure limit determined using this three-year average gross revenue structure instead of taxable capital (ITA s. 127(10.2))—an advantageous election for capital-intensive biotechnology, hardware, or clean-technology CCPCs that hold over $15,000,000 in balance-sheet capital while remaining pre-revenue or low-revenue:

where A is nil ($0) if the 3-year average annual gross revenue is ≤ $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which the 3-year average annual gross revenue exceeds $15,000,000. Once 3-year average annual gross revenue reaches $75,000,000, the expenditure limit is nil ($0), and all qualified expenditures earn only the basic 15% non-refundable ITC.
3.4 Qualifying Corporation Status, the Qualifying Income Limit, and Refundability Matrix

Under section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, the cash refundability of an earned SR&ED ITC depends on three variables: the legal status of the claimant (CCPC, ECPC, individual, trust, partnership, or other corporation), whether the ITC was earned at the 35% enhanced rate (within the expenditure limit) or the 15% basic rate (above the expenditure limit), and whether the underlying expenditure is of a current nature (including the Prescribed Proxy Amount [PPA]) or of a capital nature.

A frequent point of confusion in R&D tax audits is the statutory distinction between a CCPC that is a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) and a CCPC that is not a qualifying corporation under subsection 127.1(2.01). Under subsection 127.1(2.01) (for CCPCs) and amended subsection 127.1(2) (for ECPCs), every CCPC and ECPC (other than an "excluded corporation") receives a 100% cash refund on the unclaimed balance of its 35% enhanced ITC earned on current expenditures and the PPA, and a 40% cash refund on its 35% enhanced ITC earned on capital expenditures, regardless of its prior-year taxable income. However, if a CCPC spends more than its $6,000,000 expenditure limit (or has a reduced expenditure limit), its excess qualified expenditures earn the 15% basic ITC. That 15% basic ITC is 40% refundable only if the CCPC is a "qualifying corporation"—meaning its taxable income (together with associated corporations) for the preceding taxation year did not exceed its "qualifying income limit". For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the qualifying income limit is $500,000 of prior-year taxable income, reduced by the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital formula:

body.text: 3.5 Carryforwards, Carrybacks, and Taxability of Federal and Provincial Credits

Any portion of an SR&ED ITC that is not applied to reduce Part I tax payable in the current year and is not refunded in cash (under subsection 127.1(3), refunded ITCs are deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax) may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years (10 years for credits earned prior to 2006). Unclaimed balances in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures carry forward indefinitely to reduce taxable business income in future taxation years, except for partnerships, which cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool and must deduct 100% of the pool in computing partnership net income in the year incurred.
The taxability and pool reduction mechanics of federal and provincial R&D credits operate across three statutory rules under paragraphs 37(1)(d), 12(1)(t), 12(1)(v), and 12(1)(x):

items: Current-Year Reduction for Provincial and Territorial Credits (ITA s. 37(1)(d) & s. 127(9)): Provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (such as Ontario's OITC/ORDTC, Québec's CRIC, BC's SR&ED credit, or Alberta's IEG) constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9). Consequently, any provincial R&D credit that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its filing-due date reduces both the current-year Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Line 429 of Form T661) under paragraph 37(1)(d) (on a project-by-project basis down to nil) and the current-year federal qualified expenditures (Lines 513–515) before the federal 35% or 15% ITC is calculated.

Income Inclusion for Provincial Credits Earned on the Notional PPA (ITA s. 12(1)(x)): When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is a notional figure included in qualified expenditures for ITC calculation, but it is not included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool. Because assistance reduces the Section 37 pool only to the extent that the expenditures for which the assistance was given were included in the pool, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit attributable to the PPA cannot reduce the Section 37 pool; instead, it must be included directly in the taxpayer's income in the year received under paragraph 12(1)(x) on Schedule 1 of the T2 corporate income tax return.

Subsequent-Year Pool Reduction for Federal ITCs (Line 435 & ITA s. 12(1)(v)): Unlike provincial tax credits (which reduce the federal pool in the current year), a federal SR&ED ITC that is applied against Part I tax, carried back, or refunded in cash in Year 1 reduces the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in Year 2 (the immediately following taxation year) on Line 435 of Form T661. If the deductions from the Section 37 pool exceed the available pool balance, the negative balance is included in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(v) (alongside paragraph 12(1)(t) rules) and added back to the pool in the subsequent year.

body.text: 4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methods, and Recapture Rules

Once a project passes the technical eligibility threshold of subsection 248(1), the claimant must quantify its allowable SR&ED expenditures (Part 3 of Form T661) and its total qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (Part 4 of Form T661).
4.1 Salaries and Wages (Lines 300 to 315)

Salaries and wages represent the largest expenditure component of most Canadian SR&ED claims and are governed by the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy. Under both the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method, the claimant may include on Line 300 (non-specified employees) and Line 305 (specified employees) the portion of salaries or wages paid to employees for the time they were directly engaged in SR&ED. Being "directly engaged" refers to hands-on technical work and is determined by the tasks performed, not by the employee's corporate job title. Salaries of employees who support SR&ED but are not directly engaged (such as clerical, administrative, or purchasing staff), as well as the employer's share of related payroll benefits, cannot be claimed on Lines 300/305; they can only be claimed on Line 360 under the Traditional Method (if directly related and incremental) and are excluded under the Proxy Method (where they are covered by the 55% PPA).

Special statutory limits apply to specified employees—defined in subsection 248(1) as any employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation:

items: No Bonuses or Profit-Based Remuneration: Bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are excluded for specified employees.

5 × YMPE Maximum SR&ED Salary Cap (Line 305 — ITA s. 37(9.1)): Under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum SR&ED salary or wages that can be claimed on Line 305 for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee. For a 2026 taxation year-end, the CPP YMPE is $74,600, establishing a maximum allowable SR&ED salary cap of $373,000 (5 × $74,600) per specified employee. If a specified employee performs SR&ED for associated corporations, the cap must be allocated using Form T1174.

PPA Salary Base Cap (75% / 2.5 × YMPE — ITR s. 2900(7)–(8)): A specified employee's inclusion in the Proxy Method salary base is further restricted to the lesser of 75% of total salary or 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500 in 2026).

body.text: For work outside Canada, salaries or wages paid for SR&ED performed outside Canada (Lines 307 and 309) qualify only if the work was performed directly by an employee resident in Canada, the work was undertaken solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada, the pay is not taxed by another country, and the combined foreign SR&ED salary does not exceed 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada (Line 300 + Line 305). Finally, under the 180-day unpaid remuneration rule (ITA s. 78(4)), any salary or wages incurred in the taxation year that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year. They must be reported on Line 315 of Form T661 in the year incurred and can only be claimed on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (and remain permanently excluded from the PPA salary base under Regulation 2900(9)).
4.2 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)

Under subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must elect on Form T661 for each taxation year whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the Proxy Method (Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Line 162). If no election is made, the Traditional Method applies automatically; once Form T661 is filed for the year, the choice is irrevocable.

Under the Proxy Method, subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations establishes the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 as 55% of the claimant's eligible SR&ED salary base, entered on Line 502. (Any reference to a 65% or 60% proxy rate is outdated; the statutory PPA rate was 65% for 2012 and prior years, 60% for 2013, and has been 55% since 2014). The PPA is a notional substitute for overhead and other expenditures. It is added to qualified expenditures in Part 4 to earn the 35% or 15% federal ITC, but it is never added to the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the claimant deducts its actual underlying overhead expenses as regular business expenses. Under Regulation 2900(9), for all employees (regular and specified), the PPA salary base (Line 810 less Line 812) cannot include taxable benefits (under sections 6 or 7), bonuses, remuneration based on profits, prior-year unpaid salaries paid in the year (Line 310), or employer contributions for related benefits.

For each specified employee (Lines 850 to 860), Regulation 2900(7) restricts the maximum amount included in the PPA salary base to the lesser of: (1) directly engaged SR&ED salary (Line 856), (2) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid amounts), or (3) 2.5 × YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days of employment in the year (Line 858 = 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365), with no proration for days the individual was not a specified employee). For a 2026 taxation year-end (YMPE = $74,600), this cap is $186,500 (2.5 × $74,600) for a full year of employment. The total PPA is further limited by the overall cap in Regulation 2900(6) (Overall Cap = A − B − C, where A is total business deductions claimed in computing net income for tax purposes including cost of goods sold, B is specific statutory deductions under sections 20 [CCA, interest, bad debts], 24, 26, 30, 32, 37 [SR&ED pool], 66–66.8, and 104, and C is building use/right-to-use expenses), which generally does not restrict the PPA if the claimant deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED expenses for each $100 of eligible salary in the salary base.

Under the Traditional Method, no PPA is calculated (Line 502 = $0). Instead, the claimant tracks and claims actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360. Pursuant to the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, an overhead expense qualifies under paragraph 2900(2)(c) or subsection 2900(3) only if it satisfies two cumulative tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must connect directly—without an intervening step or intermediary—to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED, using a reasonable allocation method.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure (or allocated portion) would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred.

body.text: Under Section 4.5 of the CRA policy, recruitment expenses—including headhunter fees, job advertising, interview travel, and immigration or work permit costs—are deductible only as regular business expenses and do not qualify as SR&ED overhead. Conversely, moving expenses to relocate a selected candidate or transfer SR&ED employees to another facility within Canada, as well as related taxable housing-loss benefits, do qualify on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental. Similarly, SR&ED training costs (Section 6.5) and incremental portions of retiring allowances (Section 4.4) qualify only under the Traditional Method.

body.text: 4.3 Cloud Computing, AWS/Azure/GCP Infrastructure, and Software Licences

A major technical audit issue in modern artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and data analytics SR&ED claims is the treatment of cloud computing expenses (such as Amazon Web Services [AWS], Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud Platform [GCP] compute instances) and software subscriptions. While a vendor blog claims that cloud computing costs can be claimed as "materials consumed", CPA and tax advisory guidance establishes that cloud subscriptions and server hosting are overhead expenses that are claimable only under the Traditional Method, not under the Proxy Method. Under the Proxy Method, actual overhead is not identified at all because the 55% PPA stands in for it, meaning a cloud invoice cannot also be claimed. Under the Traditional Method, incremental cloud computing costs directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED (such as compute-heavy environments where cloud spend exceeds 55% of the salary base) are claimable on Line 360. Conversely, fixed monthly payments for internet, cellular, or telephone services that would have been incurred by the business regardless of whether SR&ED was performed fail the incremental test and are disallowed. For a team of five engineers at $600,000 of eligible salary, the Proxy Method yields $330,000 of notional overhead (55% × $600,000), making the choice between Proxy and Traditional an arithmetic comparison against provable incremental cloud/overhead spend. Additionally, per the updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), expenditures for computer software, systems software, and software licences acquired after December 15, 2024, must be evaluated to determine whether they represent a current expense or a capital expenditure based on capital cost allowance prescribed classes.
4.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Lines 320 & 325)
Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations, claimants may deduct and earn ITCs on two distinct categories of physical materials:

items: Materials Consumed (Line 320): Materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless in performing SR&ED. Note that general lab supplies such as cleaning supplies, solvents, and test tubes are classified as overhead, not materials.

Materials Transformed (Line 325): Materials or purchased components incorporated into a prototype, pilot plant, or experimental product that retains value or may later be sold or converted to commercial use (including recycled SR&ED materials), which remain subject to ITC recapture under subsection 127(27).

body.text: 4.5 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Rules, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts an arm's-length Canadian "taxable supplier" (Line 340 — ITA s. 37(1)(a)(i.01) & s. 127(9)) to perform SR&ED in Canada directly on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, but only 80% qualifies for the federal ITC (20% is subtracted on Line 529 of Form T661). Any offshore portion performed outside Canada does not qualify for the Section 37 pool or ITCs. Note that for contracts and third-party payments incurred after December 15, 2024, the former capital look-through rule (former ITA ss. 37(14) and 37(15)) no longer reduces current contract expenditures by capital expenditures of the performer.

Where a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer (Line 345 — ITA s. 127(9), (11.6), (13)), the payment is deductible in the payer's Section 37 pool (Line 345), but earns no ITC (0%) for the payer. Instead, the NAL performer (whose receipt is not treated as a "contract payment" reduction) claims the underlying SR&ED costs, or the NAL performer and payer can jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13) to transfer the qualified expenditures (Lines 508 / 544). Partnerships cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures under subsection 127(13). Furthermore, when a claimant purchases goods or services from a non-arm's length supplier, subsection 127(11.6) caps the qualified expenditure at the cost to the NAL supplier (Line 542).

Third-party payments (Line 370 — ITA s. 37(1)(a)(i.1)–(iii)) made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit SR&ED corporations for SR&ED in Canada related to the claimant's business (where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results) also enter the Section 37 pool at 100% and earn ITCs at 80% (Line 529 strips 20%), requiring Form T1263 for each payment. Finally, under subsection 127(26) (Line 520), any current expenditure other than salary or wages that remains unpaid 180 days after year-end is deducted from qualified expenditures on Line 520 and added back on Line 500 in the year paid (at 80% for arm's-length contracts), provided it was reported on Form T661 by the 18-month reporting deadline.
4.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs

Following a decade-long exclusion (2014–2024), Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of capital property and lease costs effective December 16, 2024, governed by the updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026):

items: ASA Capital Property (Line 390 — ITA s. 37(1)(b) & s. 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) / (B)(III)): Applies to new or used depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (ITA s. 37(1.2)) where the claimant intends at acquisition to use the property all or substantially all (ASA = 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada, or to consume 90% or more (ASA) of its value in SR&ED in Canada. Land, leasehold interests in land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are excluded (and under the Proxy Method, general-purpose office equipment or furniture is excluded). Used property qualifies for the Section 37 deduction on Line 390 but is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902(b) that does not earn an ITC and must be removed on Line 532. Property claimed on Line 390 must be kept off Schedule T2SCH8 (CCA).

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Line 504 & Part 6C — ITA s. 127(9)): New depreciable equipment (excluding buildings, leasehold interests, or prescribed property) acquired after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA test but is used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada is depreciated on Schedule T2SCH8 (not included in the Section 37 pool), while 25% of its capital cost earns an ITC in the first period (first-term SUE) and 25% in the second period (second-term SUE) on Line 504 (Box 792 in Part 6C).

Equipment Lease Costs (Lines 350, 355 & 360): Applies to lease costs first payable after December 15, 2024 (building leases remain excluded). Equipment leased and used ≥90% (ASA) for SR&ED is claimed at 100% on Line 350 (excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture under the Proxy Method). Equipment leased and used 50% to under 90% for SR&ED is claimed at 50% (1/2) on Line 355 under the Proxy Method (ITA s. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), or claimed on Line 360 as overhead (for any usage <90% if directly related and incremental) under the Traditional Method.

body.text: 4.7 Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (ITA s. 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, an earned SR&ED ITC is recaptured (added to Part I tax payable in the year, while increasing the subsequent year's Section 37 pool) if four cumulative conditions are met:

items: The claimant acquired a particular property in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (ITA s. 127(36) sets the 20-year recapture window).
The cost of the property was a qualified SR&ED expenditure (specifically ASA capital property, Shared-Use Equipment, or materials transformed).
A percentage of the property's cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC.
In the year, the claimant converts the property (or another property incorporating it) to commercial use, or disposes of it.

body.text: Salaries, wages, and overhead are never subject to recapture. Moreover, under the CRA's administrative de minimis 10% rule, recapture does not apply to scrap sales or experimental outputs if the proceeds of disposition or fair market value at conversion are less than 10% of the total cost of the property (nor to materials consumed unless proceeds such as insurance exceed 10% of cost). Similarly, non-arm's length dispositions of SR&ED capital property do not trigger immediate recapture if the property continues to qualify as ASA capital property for SR&ED in the hands of the non-arm's length purchaser (ITA s. 127(33)–(34)).
4.8 Proposed Budget 2026 Commercialization Expansion (Late 2026 Onwards)

According to CPA firm analyses of Federal Budget 2026 (tabled on November 5, 2026), the federal government proposed a $930 million five-year ($235 million/year ongoing) expansion of the SR&ED program beyond the laboratory stage to cover two categories of commercialization costs tied to an underlying eligible SR&ED project (noted in the firm's summaries as applying to taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 / December 1, 2026):

items: Initial Regulatory and Certification Testing: Tests, technological validations, and studies required to meet regulatory requirements for the initial approval or certification of a new product or process developed through eligible SR&ED (claimable across salaries, materials, contracts, overhead, and machinery/equipment; routine compliance testing, annual surveillance audits, and re-certification after supplier changes are excluded).

Intellectual Property (IP) Protection: Costs of registering and maintaining IP protection—including patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software—under Canadian or equivalent foreign law (administrative fees paid to foreign IP offices qualify, provided supporting application preparation work is conducted in Canada).

body.text: 5. Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Audit Defence
5.1 Dual-Track Governance: Department of Finance and the CRA

Administration of the federal SR&ED program is divided between the Department of Finance Canada (which drafts legislation for the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations) and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) (which manages intake, pre-claim approvals, and audits). Eighty percent of all SR&ED claims are filed electronically using CRA-approved commercial tax software and loaded directly onto the CRA's CORTAX mainframe, while the remaining 20% are entered manually at tax centres. T2 SR&ED claims undergo an automated preliminary risk assessment using the CRA's SR&ED risk management tool, which creates cases in the Audit Information Management System (AIMS). Roughly 40% of corporate SR&ED claims sent to tax centres are accepted as filed based on this automated preliminary risk assessment without human input. Claims selected for field review at Tax Services Offices are examined by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) (who assess technical eligibility under the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors) and Financial Reviewers (who verify expenditures under the Financial Claim Review Manual – Review Procedures for Financial Reviewers).

body.text: 5.4 Statutory Reporting Deadlines and the 90-Day Deficiency Rule

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), the SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the filing-due date of the taxpayer's income tax return for the year. For corporations (ITA s. 150(1)(a)), because the T2 return is due 6 months after year-end, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (e.g., for a December 31, 2025 year-end, the T2 is due June 30, 2026, and Form T661 + Schedule 31 are due June 30, 2027). For individuals (ITA s. 150(1)(d)(ii)), whose business T1 return is due June 15, the reporting deadline is 17.5 months after calendar year-end (June 15 of the second calendar year following the taxation year). For trusts (ITA s. 150(1)(c)), whose T3 return is due 90 days after year-end, the reporting deadline is 15 months after the trust's tax year-end. For non-profit SR&ED corporations, Form T661 is due 6 months after year-end.

There is no statutory mechanism to extend the 18-month reporting deadline. Under subsection 37(11.1), failing to report an expenditure on Form T661 with all prescribed information by the reporting deadline permanently disqualifies the expenditure from SR&ED treatment. A letter expressing an "intent to file" or a form using estimates does not satisfy the statutory filing requirement. Per the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, if a claim is submitted at least 90 days before the SR&ED reporting deadline, the CRA has sufficient time to conduct an initial completeness review and advise the claimant of any missing prescribed information so deficiencies can be cured before the 18-month deadline expires. Supporting records must be retained for 6 years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate.
5.5 New CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and Service Standards

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval process, introduced in the Canada Strong Budget 2025. Pre-claim approval is open to businesses operating in Canada that are CCPCs, Canadian corporations, or Canadian partnerships, have less than $25,000,000 in annual gross business income, are in good standing with the CRA, and submit projects not currently under objection or litigation. The process follows four steps:

items: Open a Pre-Claim Approval Request: Complete the web form on Canada.ca to receive a Case Number in My Business Account within 2 business days (existing claimants) or a CRA phone call within 5 business days (new claimants).
Apply in My Business Account: Submit the application using existing project documentation for up to 3 planned projects before starting work or incurring costs.
Meet with a CRA SR&ED Specialist (RTA): Scheduled within 4 weeks of submission (mandatory for new claimants; optional/as-needed for existing claimants in good standing).
Receive Determination Within 8 Weeks: The CRA issues a formal written determination within 8 weeks of completing the application. If granted, pre-claim approval is valid for up to 3 years.

body.text: Even when pre-claim approval is granted, the claimant must still submit Form T661 (ticking Line 212 and entering the Case Number on Line 214) after the work is undertaken. The CRA's processing service standards for refundable claims (aimed to be met 90% of the time) are 60 calendar days for claims accepted as filed, 90 calendar days (cut in half from 180 days) for claims selected for expenditure review that contain only projects granted Pre-Claim Approval, and 180 calendar days for reviewed claims containing any project without Pre-Claim Approval or where work materially differed from the pre-approved scope. If a claimant disagrees with a review, it may escalate concerns to the Research and Technology Manager or Financial Review Manager (including via Form RC532, Request for Administrative Review), file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, and subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.
6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credits & Stacking Mechanics

Nine Canadian provinces and Yukon offer dedicated R&D tax credits that stack on top of the federal SR&ED ITC, while Prince Edward Island (PEI), Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer an R&D tax credit. Except where renounced on time, provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, reducing the federal qualified expenditure pool (Line 515 / Line 429 of Form T661) before the federal 35% or 15% ITC is computed.
6.1 Québec: The New CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025) and Abolished Legacy Credits

Any report citing Québec's former 14%/30% R&D salary tax credit (Form RD-222 / CO-1029.8.36.DA) as the active regime for current taxation years is outdated. In the March 25, 2025 Québec Budget, the Québec government introduced the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), effective for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025. Concurrently, Revenu Québec confirmed the elimination of seven legacy innovation tax measures (counted as eight separate legacy credits/measures in consultancy guides):

items: The tax credit for salaries and wages of R&D researchers (Form RD-222 / CO-1029.8.36.DA).
The tax credit for university research or research carried out by an eligible public research centre or research consortium (Form CO-1029.8.36.II).
The tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium.
The tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research.
The tax credit for technological adaptation services.
The industrial design component of the design tax credits (expenditures for the fashion design component remain eligible and unchanged).
The personal income tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts.

body.text: Claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (Form RD-1029.8.CR), the CRIC is 100% refundable for all eligible corporations operating a business and maintaining an establishment in Québec—including CCPCs, large public corporations, and foreign-owned subsidiaries, regardless of corporate asset size. It provides a 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the applicable exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable rate on all qualified expenditures exceeding $1,000,000. Beyond core R&D activities (harmonized with federal SR&ED definitions and scientifically reviewed by the CRA), the CRIC covers eligible pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec as a continuation of or in conjunction with Québec R&D: (a) regulatory tests, technological validations, and studies aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation; (b) product design (development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials); and (c) quality control system implementation required for initial regulatory approval or certification.

Qualified CRIC expenditures in Québec comprise: 100% of salaries and wages of employees; 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for contracts carried out in Québec; 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, eligible research consortium, or eligible university entity; and 100% of capital property acquisition costs for new depreciable equipment used in R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec, excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings (cannot be combined with Québec's C3i credit or the large investment project tax holiday on the same property). Qualified expenditures must exceed an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec personal income tax basic personal amount ($18,571 in 2025) per employee adjusted for the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. For Québec's Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI), the nexus ratio for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, uses R&D expenditures giving entitlement to the CRIC (excluding pre-commercialization costs and without subtracting the CRIC exclusion threshold).
6.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC
Administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) (ORDTC: sections 38 to 45; OITC: section 96; OBRITC: section 97), Ontario provides three R&D tax credits:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566 / T2SCH566, filed with T2SCH31): An 8% refundable tax credit on qualified current SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to a $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit (maximum $240,000/year cash credit). Ontario has not adopted the federal $6,000,000 limit or restored capital expenditures into the OITC base. The $3,000,000 limit phases out multiplicatively when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or prior-year specified/taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508 / T2SCH508): A 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures with no expenditure cap (carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years). Crucially, the OITC is government assistance for ORDTC purposes and reduces the ORDTC expenditure base before the 3.5% rate is applied (yielding a combined Ontario rate of 8% + (3.5% × 92%) = 11.22%).

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules 568 & 569): A 20% refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures under an eligible contract with an Ontario Eligible Research Institute (ERI) (universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, or Networks of Centres of Excellence) up to a $20,000,000 annual contract cap shared among associated corporations (maximum $4,000,000/year credit).

body.text: 6.3 British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Canada, and Yukon

Across Western, Prairie, Atlantic, and Northern Canada, provincial responses to the federal Bill C-15 reforms vary significantly. British Columbia (Form T666, Income Tax Act (BC), ss. 97–103) expressly aligned with the federal post-December 15, 2024 changes: qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn a 10% refundable credit up to the increased $6,000,000 expenditure limit (maximum $600,000/year, subject to the $15M–$75M taxable capital phase-out and including restored capital expenditures), while non-CCPC/non-ECPC claimants or excess expenditures earn a 10% non-refundable credit (carryback 3 years, carryforward 10 years). BC Budget 2026 made the BC credit permanent. Alberta (AT1 Schedule 29 & Form AT4970, Alberta Corporate Tax Act, ss. 26.95–26.99) operates its independent Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), paying an 8% refundable grant on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's 2-year historical average base spending level and 20% (8% + 12%) on incremental spending above that base, capped at $4,000,000 in annual spending (maximum $800,000/year grant), due 15 months after the AT1 filing-due date.

Saskatchewan (Schedule T2SCH403, The Income Tax Act (SK), ss. 63–63.4) expanded its CCPC refundable tier for qualifying expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024, from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 at 10% refundable (maximum $200,000 cash), with a 10% non-refundable credit (carryback 3 years, carryforward 10 years) on excess CCPC spending and for non-CCPCs (ECPCs do not get refundability in SK), subject to a $1,000,000 total annual credit cap. Manitoba (Schedule T2SCH380, Income Tax Act (MB), s. 7.3) provides a 15% credit on current and non-building capital R&D expenditures, which is 50% refundable (7.5%) and 50% non-refundable (7.5%) (carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years) for in-house R&D and 100% refundable (15%) for contracts with qualifying Manitoba research institutes. Finally, New Brunswick (T2SCH360), Nova Scotia (T2SCH340), Newfoundland and Labrador (T2SCH301 / T1129, where provincial eligible expenditures are not reduced by government assistance), and Yukon (T2SCH442 / T1232, Income Tax Act (Yukon), s. 15; 15% plus an additional 5% on payments to Yukon University) all provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit.

body.text: 6.4 Worked Mathematical Stacking Illustrations (Federal + Provincial)

Because provincial R&D tax credits reduce the federal qualified expenditure pool under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act, federal and provincial percentages do not simply add together. The following three mathematical models demonstrate the exact statutory calculation order:

items: Case 1 — Ontario CCPC Claiming OITC, ORDTC, and Enhanced Federal SR&ED ($1,000,000 Qualified Pool): Assume an Ontario-based qualifying CCPC incurs $1,000,000 in qualified current SR&ED expenditures (salaries, 55% PPA, materials, and 80% of an arm's-length Ontario contract) in its 2026 taxation year, with prior-year taxable income of $300,000 (< $500,000) and prior-year taxable capital of $5,000,000 (< $15,000,000). First, the OITC (Schedule 566) is $1,000,000 × 8% = $80,000 (100% refundable cash). Second, the ORDTC (Schedule 508) base is reduced by the OITC to $920,000 ($1,000,000 − $80,000), yielding $920,000 × 3.5% = $32,200 (non-refundable Ontario credit; combined Ontario credits = $112,200, or 11.22%). Third, the net Federal Qualified Expenditure Pool (Form T661, Line 570) is reduced by both Ontario credits to $887,800 ($1,000,000 − $112,200), yielding an Enhanced Federal ITC (Schedule 31) of $887,800 × 35% = $310,730 (100% refundable cash). Total combined credits equal $422,930 (42.293% of the qualified pool), of which $390,730 (39.073%) is paid in cash.

Case 2 — Québec CCPC Claiming the New CRIC and Enhanced Federal SR&ED ($1,000,000 Direct R&D Salaries): Assume a Montréal-based qualifying CCPC incurs $1,000,000 in directly engaged Québec R&D salaries across 5 full-time R&D engineers in a taxation year beginning after March 25, 2025, electing the Proxy Method. First, the Québec CRIC Exclusion Threshold is the greater of $50,000 or 5 × $18,571 (2025 Québec basic personal amount) = $92,855. Second, the Québec CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T) at 30% on qualified expenditures above the threshold ($1,000,000 − $92,855 = $907,145) equals $272,143.50 (100% refundable cash). Third, the Gross Federal Qualified Pool including the 55% PPA is $1,550,000 ($1,000,000 salaries + $550,000 PPA), which is reduced by the $272,143.50 CRIC assistance to a Net Federal Pool of $1,277,856.50. Fourth, the Enhanced Federal ITC (35%) on $1,277,856.50 equals $447,249.78 (100% refundable cash), resulting in a total combined cash refund of $719,393.28 (71.94% of the $1,000,000 direct salary outlay).

Case 3 — Nova Scotia / Atlantic Canada ($1,000,000 Qualified Pool — CCPC vs. Foreign Subsidiary): For $1,000,000 of qualified current expenditures in Nova Scotia (where the provincial credit is 15% fully refundable for all corporations): a Qualifying CCPC earns $150,000 provincially ($1,000,000 × 15%), reducing the federal pool to $850,000, which earns $297,500 federally ($850,000 × 35%), for a combined refundable cash recovery of $447,500 (44.75%). A Foreign-Controlled Subsidiary earns the same $150,000 refundable provincial credit plus $127,500 in non-refundable federal basic ITC ($850,000 × 15%), for a combined credit of $277,500 (27.75%).

body.text: 7. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents

In Canada, the statutory interpretation of subsection 248(1) and the evidentiary standards governing CRA technical audits are controlled by binding jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).
7.1 Foundational Appellate and Tax Court Authorities (1997–2016)

In Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, 97 DTC 724 (TCC), the Tax Court established the foundational purposive canon of interpretation for SR&ED: because the tax incentives for doing SR&ED are intended by Parliament to encourage scientific research in Canada, courts and administrators should not apply an overly narrow or pedantic interpretation that defeats that legislative purpose. The following year, in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC), Chief Justice Donald Bowman articulated the governing Five Criteria Test (see Section 2.3) and noted that while the Income Tax Act and Regulations do not state it explicitly, it is self-evident that a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results must be kept continuously as the work progresses.

In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890 (FCA), the Federal Court of Appeal formally endorsed Northwest Hydraulic at the appellate level and ruled under Question 5 that documentary evidence of scientific research testing and results must be adduced by the taxpayer to demonstrate repeatability. Shortly thereafter, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 (aff'g 2000 DTC 2372 (TCC)), the FCA summarized the five Northwest Hydraulic questions in their modern form. At trial in C.W. Agencies, rather than calling the project manager or programmers personally involved in designing the software, the appellant relied on an external expert witness (Dr. Slonim) who examined the finished code and conjectured what uncertainties the appellant must have faced; the Court held that post-hoc expert conjecture cannot substitute for firsthand evidence of what was actually done.

In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355, 2012 DTC 5031, involving a manufacturer of engineered thermoformed plastic products and window coverings, both Courts held that shop-floor product and process optimization conducted through routine engineering without formulating and testing hypotheses aimed at resolving technological uncertainty does not qualify as SR&ED. Similarly, in Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 DTC 1089 (TCC), the Tax Court dismissed a software claim for website inspection software because the work constituted normal analyses carried out by competent programmers using current technology and techniques. Conversely, in a 2014 Tax Court decision authored by Justice Jorré involving a Montréal-area dryer-part sub-assembly corporation (Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc.), the Court allowed the appeal for four production-line optimization projects, emphasizing two vital principles: first, expert witnesses owe a strict duty of impartiality to the Court, and second, contemporaneous documentation is not a condition sine qua non to an SR&ED claim being allowed if the totality of the evidence proves the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria. In R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada, 2015 TCC 108, aff'd 2016 FCA 152, the FCA again endorsed the Northwest Hydraulic framework in dismissing unsupported consulting claims.
7.2 Modern Appellate and Tax Court Decisions (2019–2025)

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2019 TCC 246, aff'd 2021 FCA 88 (decided May 10, 2021), the appellant argued before the Federal Court of Appeal that because the text of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act does not explicitly contain the words "scientific method," the Tax Court erred in applying Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic. Writing for the FCA, Justice Webb rejected this argument, holding that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria—including adherence to the objective principles of the scientific method—were repeatedly endorsed by the FCA in RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, Jentel Manufacturing, and R&D Pro-Innovation and remain binding law. The following year, in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2020 TCC 47, aff'd 2022 FCA 72 (decided May 2022, per Justice Rennie), the FCA upheld the denial of SR&ED credits for a consulting firm's software project ("PTS-Project"), confirming that Northwest Hydraulic applies equally to applied sciences and ruling that a taxpayer cannot use an expert witness report as an advocate to establish unproven facts "through the back door".

By contrast, two recent Tax Court of Canada decisions demonstrate how food and beverage manufacturers can successfully defeat overly rigid CRA audit denials. In Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC), a frozen pie manufacturer contested the CRA's disallowance of seven SR&ED projects across 2013–2016 (representing $343,449 in denied expenditures and $60,963 in ITCs excluding 2014) aimed at extending shelf life without preservatives, reducing salt and fat using real potatoes and antibiotic-free meat, and maintaining product integrity after blast-freezing and reheating. Finding the CEO's testimony and detailed trial documentation compelling and forthright, the Tax Court allowed the appeal in full. Most recently, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, Docket 2023-2126(IT)I (TCC, decided January 17, 2025, per Justice Bodie), the taxpayer appealed the denial of its 2020 SR&ED claim for developing "Chrisoda," a shelf-stable, non-refrigerated vinegar-based beverage where the appellant systematically tested potassium sorbate, sodium benzoate, and a natural preservative ("Chiber") to control microbial growth. Allowing the appeal, Justice Bodie established three crucial audit principles: (1) a technological uncertainty can be established even where a publicly available solution exists, provided it has never been used in the specific context; (2) contemporaneous documentation is meant to track hypotheses, tests, and results as work progresses and does not need to be written for an outside stranger unfamiliar with the field to replicate results; and (3) despite the CRA's 2021 "Why and How" guidelines, the five Northwest Hydraulic questions remain the valid judicial test for SR&ED eligibility.
